claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a homogeneous, single-phase fcc matrix.
The starting alloy contains minimal or negligible pre-existing oxide.
Elevated-temperature degradation in the target alloy is governed by sequential element-specific oxidation that creates a layered scale.
Oxidation of the target alloy initially produces a Ni-rich inner pre-oxide layer.
Rapid Ni diffusion is responsible for formation of the initial Ni-rich layer.
The Ni-rich initial layer promotes nucleation of a subsequent chromium-oxide layer.
The middle layer is protective Cr2O3.
Continued oxidation produces an outer oxide enriched in Fe, Co, and Ti.
Fe, Co, and Ti diffuse more slowly than Ni, and this diffusivity difference drives their buildup in the outer oxide.
The Fe/Co/Ti-rich outer oxide is less protective and less adherent than the inner layers.
Development of the outer oxide eventually causes scale spallation and loss of long-term integrity.
A reducing atmosphere limits or suppresses oxide formation relative to an oxidizing atmosphere.
Reduced oxide formation delays degradation and improves retention of the baseline alloy microstructure.
Under oxidizing conditions, oxide-scale thickness increases with exposure time.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply around 400 °C and an oxygen partial pressure near 10 mbar.
Significantly higher temperatures or different gas compositions may alter oxidation kinetics and phase stability, potentially inducing phase transformations.
A controlled comparison at approximately 400 °C between 10 mbar O2 and a reducing or inert environment over 2, 30, and 120 minutes can distinguish the proposed mechanism.
Cross-sectional TEM, EDS mapping, oxide-thickness measurements, weight gain, and spallation assessment can test the predicted scale evolution.
Absence of the predicted Ni-rich/Cr2O3/Fe-Co-Ti layered sequence, or similar oxide characteristics and degradation rates in both gas environments, would falsify the hypothesis.
The role of Ti in scale formation and adhesion is unresolved.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism say that limited oxidation under reducing conditions preserves the layered or protective layers, whereas the predicted outcome says those conditions produce thinner or incomplete oxide layers. It is unclear how a layered protective structure is preserved if it is suppressed or incomplete.
